the use of the Roche Modular E170 analyzer for thyroid analyte measurements in elderly subjects is feasible and that the reference ranges need to be adjusted according to age and gender.

the reference intervals for thyroid function tests in the healthy elderly are higher than those in the healthy younger adults, and that the age-related increase of the reference intervals in the healthy elderly is more pronounced in women than in men.

(1) the reference intervals of thyroid hormones in the elderly should be different than those in the young; (2) the TSH reference interval should be wider in the elderly than in the young; and (3) the reference intervals for thyroid hormones and TSH should be different for men and women.

a study of the relationship between the age of a person and their gender, and the amount of the thyroid hormones TSH, FT4 and FT3 in their serum.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the use of age and gender dependent TSH and FT4 reference intervals for the interpretation of the thyroid function tests is not necessary and that the age and gender independent TSH reference intervals can be used in the elderly.
there are no age- and sex-dependent reference ranges for TSH, FT4, FT3 and T3RU in healthy elderly subjects.
, in healthy subjects, the reference interval of TSH is age and gender independent and should be set at 0.3-4.2 mU/L.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the thyroid hormones TSH, FT4, and FT3 are not significantly different in the elderly and young subjects when the data are adjusted for body weight and body mass index.
there are no differences in the levels of TSH, FT4 and FT3 between the elderly and younger subjects, but that the reference levels for TSH and FT4 should be lower and for FT3 higher.
we have shown that the thyroid hormones T4, T3 and TSH are all regulated by the thyroid hormones TSH and T4, and that the thyroid hormone T4 is regulated by the thyroid hormone T3.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the thyroid hormone T4 has a much greater effect on the brain than T3.
the thyroid gland plays a role in brain development, and that thyroid hormones may have a direct impact on brain function.
the thyroid gland is a major contributor to the regulation of body temperature, and the thyroid hormone triiodothyronine (T3) is a critical mediator of this effect.
